opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, and I'd say I'm fairly, but not overwhelmingly, confident that more people working on this is good on net. I wouldn't say it's a slam dunk.

The case for "obviously good" is simple: this could be one of the most important things happening in the world, and relative to the stakes, very few people are working seriously on making it go well. Alignment research, interpretability, evaluations, security, policy: in all of these I see far more good, tractable work than people to do it. So the naive answer is that adding talent should help.

But I take the downside cases seriously. One is that people who come in worried about AI risk end up accelerating the thing they worry about. They join labs, do capabilities-adjacent work, help build hype, or add to a sense that this is the important frontier technology everyone needs to race on. You can tell a story where the AI safety community, on net, has sped things up. I don't think that story is the whole picture, but I don't think it's crazy either.

Another is that a field can get bigger without getting better. You can dilute quality, or create a lot of noise, or have people pushing policy ideas that are poorly thought through and that burn credibility or trigger a backlash. Badly targeted advocacy can make the issue look partisan or fringe. And there's the risk of people working hard on approaches that give false reassurance, where we feel safer than we are.

So my view is roughly this: the expected value of more people is positive, and I'd guess substantially so, but the variance is high and much depends on what those people actually do and how careful they are. My advice to someone entering the field is less "just show up" and more: be thoughtful about whether your work differentially helps safety rather than just general progress, stay humble about your theory of change, try to work with or near people who have good judgment, and keep checking whether you're making things better. If people do that, I feel pretty good about growth. If the field grows by people charging ahead without that reflection, I'm a lot more nervous.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the expected value of adding people is positive and the variance is high, but does not state that uncorrelated or negatively correlated impacts make the probability of a positive overall impact rise further above 50% as more researchers join.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this in a few layers. The first thing I'd say is that I don't think it's a sure thing. There's a version of this where you add a bunch of people to a field, and they end up accelerating the thing you were worried about, or they end up crowding out better work, or they end up just adding noise. So I want to be honest that there's real uncertainty here, and I don't think anyone should walk in thinking "more people working on AI safety" is automatically good.

But when I actually try to weigh it, I come down pretty strongly on the side that it's beneficial in expectation. And the way I'd break it down is something like this.

The core situation, as I see it, is that we may be heading toward transformative AI on a timeline that is uncomfortably short relative to how prepared we are. And "prepared" here means a lot of things: do we have alignment techniques that actually work, do we have ways to evaluate whether a system is dangerous before we deploy it, do we have the institutional and governance machinery to respond when something goes wrong, do we have enough people who deeply understand these systems and also care about the risks. On basically every one of those dimensions, my honest assessment is that we're way behind where I'd want us to be. And the bottleneck is very often people. Not just raw headcount, but people with the right mix of skills, judgment, and motivation.

So when I imagine the counterfactual, where fewer people work on this, I don't picture a world where the problem gets solved anyway by the people already there. I picture a world where a lot of important questions just don't get worked on, or get worked on too slowly, or get worked on only by people who have strong incentives to reach convenient conclusions.

Now, the main worry people raise, and I think it's a legitimate one, is the acceleration concern. If you train a lot of people in AI and put them near frontier labs, some of them will end up pushing capabilities forward, and that could make things worse. I take that seriously. But a few things make me less worried than I might otherwise be. One is that the capabilities frontier is being pushed by an enormous amount of money and talent regardless. The marginal safety-motivated person is a small fraction of that. Two is that a lot of the most important safety work genuinely requires being close to the technology. You can't evaluate a model you can't see. Three is that I think the people who are most likely to go into this field because they're worried about the risks are also the people most likely to make good calls when they're in positions of influence. I'd rather have them in the room than not.

The other worry is something like, "What if the field is just confused, and adding people adds confusion?" And honestly, I think the field is pretty confused. But I think the response to that is to add thoughtful people who are willing to push back on consensus and do careful work, not to leave the field small. Small fields have their own pathologies. They become insular, they develop blind spots, and they're easy to dismiss.

So if I had to put a rough shape on it, I'd say: I think there's maybe a modest chance that any given person's contribution is net negative or negligible, a decent chance it's a small positive, and a meaningful tail where it's quite important, because they end up being one of the people who shapes a key decision or solves a key problem at a key moment. And when you add that up, especially given how high the stakes are, I think it's one of the better bets a person can make with their career. Not a certain one. But a good one.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that I think the question of "is it net positive" depends a lot on how people go into it. If you go in with humility, with a willingness to update, with an eye toward what's actually true rather than what's fashionable in the community, I think your expected impact is a lot higher. So part of my answer is: yes, more people should work on this, and also, how you work on it matters a lot.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the overall effect is beneficial in expectation and describes possible positive contributions, but does not state that slightly-more-likely-than-not positive individual impacts, combined with uncorrelated or negatively correlated impacts, make the probability of a positive overall impact rise further above 50% as more researchers join.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on who the people are and what they’re doing. I don’t think of AI risk as a problem where we have a well-defined list of tasks and every additional person who shows up makes things a little better. There’s still a lot of uncertainty about what the most useful work is, and some ways of trying to help could make things worse.

For example, you might do research that you think is going to make AI safer, but that mostly makes it easier to build more powerful systems. Or you might advocate for a policy that sounds sensible but ends up making it harder to adopt better policies later. So I wouldn’t equate getting more people interested in AI risk with reducing AI risk.

But I do think there’s a very strong case for getting more thoughtful people working on it—people who are willing to understand the arguments, question their own plans, and change direction. The uncertainty cuts both ways: it means we can’t be confident that a particular project will help, but it also means there’s enormous value in people who can help us figure out what to do.

So my answer is pretty positive about adding people with good judgment and a willingness to learn, and much less confident about simply trying to maximize the number of people working under the heading of AI safety.

r001.rationale: The candidate favors adding thoughtful people but does not state that each researcher is more likely than not to help, or that uncorrelated or negatively correlated impacts make the probability of an overall positive impact rise further above 50% as more researchers join.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what those people are doing. I don’t think there’s a simple relationship where more people working on something called “AI safety” necessarily means less risk. Some work could be unhelpful, and some could actually make things worse—for example, if it makes AI systems more capable without giving us a corresponding improvement in our ability to understand or control them.

But I do think there are important problems here where we’re very short of people who can do excellent work. So I’d distinguish “Can we get more people into this field?” from “Can we get more people developing good judgment about these problems and finding concrete ways to help?” I’m much more excited about the second.

For someone considering this, I wouldn’t want the whole argument to be, “AI risk is important, therefore whatever I do in this area is good.” I’d want them to have a story about what their work changes, why that change helps, and what could go wrong. There’s a lot of uncertainty, but that’s a reason to be thoughtful about the particular contribution, rather than to assume that either adding people or keeping people away is always the right answer.

r001.rationale: The response says the effect of adding researchers depends on the work and emphasizes uncertainty, but it does not state the probability argument that mostly-positive, uncorrelated or negatively correlated contributions make an overall positive impact increasingly likely as more researchers join.
